identity.title: GEPA: Reflective Prompt Evolution Can Outperform Reinforcement Learning

problem.claim: Adapt LLM-based systems to downstream tasks with fewer trial-and-error rollouts.

gap.claim: The abstract contrasts rollout-intensive RL and sparse scalar policy-gradient feedback with the richer learning signal potentially available through interpretable natural language.

contributions.claim: Introduces GEPA (Genetic-Pareto), a prompt optimizer that uses natural-language reflection to learn high-level rules from trial and error.
Defines a general procedure for sampling trajectories, diagnosing problems, proposing and testing prompt updates, and combining complementary lessons from a Pareto frontier.
Reports improvements over GRPO and MIPROv2 across multiple tasks, including promising inference-time code-optimization results.

stated_novelty.claim: The authors present GEPA as a prompt optimizer that thoroughly incorporates natural-language reflection and Pareto-frontier lesson combination.

author_reported_evidence.claim: Across six tasks, the authors report that GEPA exceeds GRPO by 6 percentage points on average and by up to 19 percentage points, while using up to 35× fewer rollouts.
The authors report that GEPA exceeds MIPROv2 by over 10 percentage points, including a 12-point improvement on AIME-2025.
The authors report promising results when using GEPA as an inference-time search strategy for code optimization.

narrative_sequence.summary: RL adaptation methods such as GRPO often require thousands of rollouts.
The authors argue that natural language can provide a richer learning medium than sparse scalar rewards.
GEPA reflects on sampled trajectories, diagnoses failures, tests prompt updates, and combines Pareto-frontier lessons.
The abstract reports fewer-rollout gains over GRPO and score improvements over MIPROv2, plus code-optimization applications.
The authors provide the implementation as open-source code.

source_observation.claim: The method links trajectory diagnosis in natural language to proposed and tested prompt updates, while retaining complementary lessons from a Pareto frontier.

lessons.interpretation: This suggests a useful design pattern for turning qualitative failure analysis into iterative optimization without collapsing all feedback into one scalar objective.
lessons.application: For a system with multiple prompts, record interpretable trajectory diagnoses, test targeted prompt edits, and preserve non-dominated improvements rather than selecting only one aggregate winner.
lessons.exception: This may be unsuitable when trajectory text is unavailable, reflection is unreliable, or the task requires a single objective and has no meaningful trade-offs.

unknowns: The abstract does not identify the six tasks, evaluation protocols, rollout budgets in absolute terms, or statistical uncertainty.
The conditions behind the reported gains and the meaning of “promising” for code optimization are unspecified.
The abstract does not provide comparative details sufficient to assess reproducibility or independent validity.
